claim: Kv3 potassium currents mediate rapid repolarisation of action potentials (APs), supporting fast spikes and high repetition rates.
source: Kv3 potassium currents mediate rapid repolarisation of action potentials (APs), supporting fast spikes and high repetition rates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature (Rudy and McBain, 2001; Kaczmarek and Zhang, 2017) and represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 are highly expressed in the auditory brainstem.
source: Of the four Kv3 gene family members, Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 are highly expressed in the auditory brainstem and we exploited this to test for subunit-specific roles at the calyx of Held presynaptic terminal in the mouse.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work (Choudhury et al., 2020) and by mRNA sequencing data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 (but not Kv3.1) reduced presynaptic Kv3 channel immunolabelling.
source: Deletion of Kv3.3 (but not Kv3.1) reduced presynaptic Kv3 channel immunolabelling, increased presynaptic AP duration and facilitated excitatory transmitter release; which in turn enhanced short-term depression during high-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2, which demonstrates differential localization of Kv3.3 and Kv3.1 subunits at the presynaptic terminal.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 increased presynaptic AP duration.
source: Deletion of Kv3.3 (but not Kv3.1) reduced presynaptic Kv3 channel immunolabelling, increased presynaptic AP duration and facilitated excitatory transmitter release; which in turn enhanced short-term depression during high-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is supported by direct electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1E, where AP half-width increased from 0.28±0.02ms in WT to 0.43±0.03ms in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 facilitated excitatory transmitter release.
source: Deletion of Kv3.3 (but not Kv3.1) reduced presynaptic Kv3 channel immunolabelling, increased presynaptic AP duration and facilitated excitatory transmitter release; which in turn enhanced short-term depression during high-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude measurements shown in Figure 3B, where EPSC amplitudes increased from –13±2 nA in WT to –18±5 nA in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 enhanced short-term depression during high-frequency transmission.
source: Deletion of Kv3.3 (but not Kv3.1) reduced presynaptic Kv3 channel immunolabelling, increased presynaptic AP duration and facilitated excitatory transmitter release; which in turn enhanced short-term depression during high-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing increased paired-pulse depression and faster short-term depression decay time constants in Kv3.3KO mice.

claim: The response to sound was delayed in the Kv3.3KO.
source: The response to sound was delayed in the Kv3.3KO, with higher spontaneous and lower evoked firing, thereby reducing signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 8, where first spike latencies increased from 3.44ms in WT to 4.06ms in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Kv3.3KO mice showed higher spontaneous firing than WT.
source: The response to sound was delayed in the Kv3.3KO, with higher spontaneous and lower evoked firing, thereby reducing signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 8L showing spontaneous firing increased from 16.5 Hz in WT to 40 Hz in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Kv3.3KO mice showed lower evoked firing than WT.
source: The response to sound was delayed in the Kv3.3KO, with higher spontaneous and lower evoked firing, thereby reducing signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 8H showing peak firing rates decreased from 350 Hz in WT to 240 Hz in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 reduced signal-to-noise ratio in auditory processing.
source: The response to sound was delayed in the Kv3.3KO, with higher spontaneous and lower evoked firing, thereby reducing signal-to-noise ratio.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 8M showing signal-to-noise ratio decreased from 9.70 in WT to 2.77 in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Computational modelling showed that the enhanced EPSC and short-term depression in the Kv3.3KO reflected increased vesicle release probability.
source: Computational modelling showed that the enhanced EPSC and short-term depression in the Kv3.3KO reflected increased vesicle release probability and accelerated activity-dependent vesicle replenishment.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B, where release probability (Pv) increased from 0.13 in WT to 0.266 in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Computational modelling showed that the enhanced EPSC and short-term depression in the Kv3.3KO reflected accelerated activity-dependent vesicle replenishment.
source: Computational modelling showed that the enhanced EPSC and short-term depression in the Kv3.3KO reflected increased vesicle release probability and accelerated activity-dependent vesicle replenishment.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B, where the activity-dependent recycling time constant (τh) decreased from 66.9 to 52.2 in Kv3.3KO.

claim: Kv3.3 mediates fast repolarisation for short precise APs, conserving transmission during sustained high-frequency activity at this glutamatergic excitatory synapse.
source: We conclude that Kv3.3 mediates fast repolarisation for short precise APs, conserving transmission during sustained high-frequency activity at this glutamatergic excitatory synapse.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including AP duration measurements, transmitter release data, short-term depression analysis, and in vivo recordings.

claim: Kv3 channels are expressed throughout the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum, and auditory brainstem.
source: Kv3 channels are expressed throughout the brain including the hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum, and auditory brainstem (Weiser et al., 1994; Du et al., 2000; Lien and Jonas, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature documenting Kv3 channel expression patterns.

claim: Kv3 channels influence dendritic integration.
source: They influence dendritic integration (Zagha et al., 2010) and somatic AP waveform (Espinosa et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2014; Choudhury et al., 2020), but Kv3 channels are also located in particular axons, including nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and synaptic terminals (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zagha et al., 2010.

claim: Kv3 channels influence somatic AP waveform.
source: They influence dendritic integration (Zagha et al., 2010) and somatic AP waveform (Espinosa et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2014; Choudhury et al., 2020), but Kv3 channels are also located in particular axons, including nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and synaptic terminals (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Espinosa et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2014; Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: Kv3 channels are located in nodes of Ranvier.
source: They influence dendritic integration (Zagha et al., 2010) and somatic AP waveform (Espinosa et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2014; Choudhury et al., 2020), but Kv3 channels are also located in particular axons, including nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and synaptic terminals (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Devaux et al., 2003.

claim: Kv3 channels are located in synaptic terminals.
source: They influence dendritic integration (Zagha et al., 2010) and somatic AP waveform (Espinosa et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2014; Choudhury et al., 2020), but Kv3 channels are also located in particular axons, including nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and synaptic terminals (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006.

claim: There are four Kv3 genes (kcnc1-4) specifying alpha subunits (Kv3.1–3.4) that assemble as tetramers.
source: There are four Kv3 genes (kcnc1-4) specifying alpha subunits (Kv3.1–3.4) that assemble as tetramers (Coetzee et al., 1999; Rudy et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coetzee et al., 1999; Rudy et al., 1999 and represents established knowledge about Kv3 channel structure.

claim: The transmembrane domains are generally well conserved across Kv3 subunits.
source: The transmembrane domains are generally well conserved across subunits, but both the N- and C-terminal domains have diverse sequences, creating distinct inactivation kinetics, interaction with cytoskeletal proteins (Blosa et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2021) and regulation by phosphorylation (Macica et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Desai et al., 2008).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Kv3 channel structure.

claim: The N- and C-terminal domains of Kv3 subunits have diverse sequences, creating distinct inactivation kinetics.
source: The transmembrane domains are generally well conserved across subunits, but both the N- and C-terminal domains have diverse sequences, creating distinct inactivation kinetics, interaction with cytoskeletal proteins (Blosa et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2021) and regulation by phosphorylation (Macica et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Desai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations documenting functional diversity.

claim: The N- and C-terminal domains of Kv3 subunits create distinct interactions with cytoskeletal proteins.
source: The transmembrane domains are generally well conserved across subunits, but both the N- and C-terminal domains have diverse sequences, creating distinct inactivation kinetics, interaction with cytoskeletal proteins (Blosa et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2021) and regulation by phosphorylation (Macica et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Desai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blosa et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2021.

claim: The N- and C-terminal domains of Kv3 subunits create distinct regulation by phosphorylation.
source: The transmembrane domains are generally well conserved across subunits, but both the N- and C-terminal domains have diverse sequences, creating distinct inactivation kinetics, interaction with cytoskeletal proteins (Blosa et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2021) and regulation by phosphorylation (Macica et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Desai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Macica et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Desai et al., 2008.

claim: Kv3 channels display ultra-fast kinetics.
source: Kv3 channels display ultra-fast kinetics (Grissmer et al., 1994; Labro et al., 2015) with half-activation at positive voltages, making them particularly effective in AP repolarisation (Brew and Forsythe, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grissmer et al., 1994; Labro et al., 2015.

claim: Kv3 channels have half-activation at positive voltages.
source: Kv3 channels display ultra-fast kinetics (Grissmer et al., 1994; Labro et al., 2015) with half-activation at positive voltages, making them particularly effective in AP repolarisation (Brew and Forsythe, 1995).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Kv3 channel biophysical properties.

claim: Kv3 channels are particularly effective in AP repolarisation.
source: Kv3 channels display ultra-fast kinetics (Grissmer et al., 1994; Labro et al., 2015) with half-activation at positive voltages, making them particularly effective in AP repolarisation (Brew and Forsythe, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brew and Forsythe, 1995 and represents established knowledge.

claim: N-type inactivation is a powerful means of regulating K+ channel activity.
source: N-type inactivation is a powerful means of regulating K+ channel activity (Hoshi et al., 1990) and inactivation in the Kv3 family is influenced by the subunit(s) expressed and their regulation by protein phosphorylation (see Kaczmarek and Zhang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoshi et al., 1990 and represents established knowledge about potassium channel regulation.

claim: Inactivation in the Kv3 family is influenced by the subunit(s) expressed and their regulation by protein phosphorylation.
source: N-type inactivation is a powerful means of regulating K+ channel activity (Hoshi et al., 1990) and inactivation in the Kv3 family is influenced by the subunit(s) expressed and their regulation by protein phosphorylation (see Kaczmarek and Zhang, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaczmarek and Zhang, 2017.

claim: Transgenic knockouts of one Kv3 subunit generally show mild phenotypes.
source: Transgenic knockouts of one subunit generally show mild phenotypes, consistent with heterogeneous composition of native channels and functional redundancy (Joho et al., 1999; Espinosa et al., 2001; Joho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joho et al., 1999; Espinosa et al., 2001; Joho et al., 2006.

claim: Mild phenotypes in Kv3 knockouts are consistent with heterogeneous composition of native channels and functional redundancy.
source: Transgenic knockouts of one subunit generally show mild phenotypes, consistent with heterogeneous composition of native channels and functional redundancy (Joho et al., 1999; Espinosa et al., 2001; Joho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and represents a mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Co-expression of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 has been widely observed in different brain regions.
source: Co-expression of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 has been widely observed in different brain regions (Chang et al., 2007) and we recently showed that principal neurons of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) within the auditory brainstem, have Kv3 channels composed of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: Principal neurons of the MNTB have Kv3 channels composed of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits.
source: Co-expression of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 has been widely observed in different brain regions (Chang et al., 2007) and we recently showed that principal neurons of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) within the auditory brainstem, have Kv3 channels composed of Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work (Choudhury et al., 2020).

claim: In the MNTB, each Kv3 subunit type can compensate for deletion of the other.
source: In the MNTB, in contrast to the lateral superior olive, each subunit type can compensate for deletion of the other (Choudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Choudhury et al., 2020).

claim: Changes in AP waveform at the synaptic terminal critically control calcium influx and neurotransmitter release.
source: Changes in AP waveform at the synaptic terminal critically control calcium influx and neurotransmitter release (Borst and Sakmann, 1998; Forsythe et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2014), this in turn influences short-term plasticity (Sakaba and Neher, 2003; Hennig et al., 2008; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Neher, 2017; Lipstein et al., 2021) and presynaptic forms of long term potentiation at mossy fiber terminals (Geiger and Jonas, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borst and Sakmann, 1998; Forsythe et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2014 and represents established knowledge.

claim: AP waveform influences short-term plasticity.
source: Changes in AP waveform at the synaptic terminal critically control calcium influx and neurotransmitter release (Borst and Sakmann, 1998; Forsythe et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2014), this in turn influences short-term plasticity (Sakaba and Neher, 2003; Hennig et al., 2008; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Neher, 2017; Lipstein et al., 2021) and presynaptic forms of long term potentiation at mossy fiber terminals (Geiger and Jonas, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sakaba and Neher, 2003; Hennig et al., 2008; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Neher, 2017; Lipstein et al., 2021.

claim: AP waveform influences presynaptic forms of long term potentiation at mossy fiber terminals.
source: Changes in AP waveform at the synaptic terminal critically control calcium influx and neurotransmitter release (Borst and Sakmann, 1998; Forsythe et al., 1998; Yang et al., 2014), this in turn influences short-term plasticity (Sakaba and Neher, 2003; Hennig et al., 2008; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Neher, 2017; Lipstein et al., 2021) and presynaptic forms of long term potentiation at mossy fiber terminals (Geiger and Jonas, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geiger and Jonas, 2000.

claim: Tuning of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channel kinetics enhances fast signaling and increases metabolic efficiency.
source: Indeed, tuning of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channel kinetics not only enhances fast signaling, but also increases metabolic efficiency (Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2018.

claim: Binaural auditory nuclei must rapidly integrate AP trains transmitted from left and right cochlea with microsecond accuracy.
source: These binaural auditory nuclei must rapidly integrate AP trains transmitted from left and right cochlea with microsecond accuracy (Beiderbeck et al., 2018; Joris and Trussell, 2018; Karcz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beiderbeck et al., 2018; Joris and Trussell, 2018; Karcz et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge about auditory processing.

claim: The MNTB region expresses Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits, with little or no Kv3.2 and Kv3.4.
source: The region expresses Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits, with little or no Kv3.2 and Kv3.4 (Choudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: The calyx of Held synapse is optimised for speed and fidelity.
source: This synapse is optimised for speed and fidelity (Taschenberger et al., 2002) and is operating at the 'biophysical limit' of information processing, in that fast conducting axons and giant synapses with nano-domain localisation of P/Q Ca2+ channels, combine with postsynaptic expression of fast AMPARs, short postsynaptic membrane time-constants and exceptionally rapid APs to enable binaural sound localisation (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Joris and Trussell, 2018; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taschenberger et al., 2002 and represents established knowledge about this synapse.

claim: The calyx of Held synapse is operating at the 'biophysical limit' of information processing.
source: This synapse is optimised for speed and fidelity (Taschenberger et al., 2002) and is operating at the 'biophysical limit' of information processing, in that fast conducting axons and giant synapses with nano-domain localisation of P/Q Ca2+ channels, combine with postsynaptic expression of fast AMPARs, short postsynaptic membrane time-constants and exceptionally rapid APs to enable binaural sound localisation (Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Joris and Trussell, 2018; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schneggenburger and Forsythe, 2006; Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Joris and Trussell, 2018; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021.

claim: Kv3.3 subunits are localised to the presynaptic terminal.
source: We show that Kv3.3 subunits are localised to the presynaptic terminal and that their deletion increases transmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 increases transmitter release.
source: We show that Kv3.3 subunits are localised to the presynaptic terminal and that their deletion increases transmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Presynaptic Kv3.3 subunits are essential for fast AP repolarisation at this excitatory synapse.
source: We demonstrate the role of Kv3.3 in enhancing the speed and reliability of brainstem binaural auditory processing and conclude that presynaptic Kv3.3 subunits are essential for fast AP repolarisation at this excitatory synapse.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including AP duration measurements, transmitter release data, and in vivo recordings.

claim: Both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 mRNA are present in the cochlear nucleus.
source: As an additional control, we confirmed that both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 mRNA are present in the cochlear nucleus where globular bushy cells give rise to the calyx of Held synaptic terminal.
evidence: This is supported by mRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Globular bushy cells in the cochlear nucleus give rise to the calyx of Held synaptic terminal.
source: As an additional control, we confirmed that both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 mRNA are present in the cochlear nucleus where globular bushy cells give rise to the calyx of Held synaptic terminal.
evidence: This represents established anatomical knowledge about the auditory brainstem.

source: The percent contribution of each subunit gene to the cochlear nucleus Kv3 mRNA was 30.3% ± 9.1% (Kv3.1), 7.7% ± 2.8% (Kv3.2), 52.0% ± 6.0% (Kv3.3), and 10.0% ± 1.6% (Kv3.4; for data see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and summary statistics).

evidence: This is supported by mRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percent contribution of Kv3.3 to cochlear nucleus Kv3 mRNA was 52.0% ± 6.0%.
source: The percent contribution of each subunit gene to the cochlear nucleus Kv3 mRNA was 30.3% ± 9.1% (Kv3.1), 7.7% ± 2.8% (Kv3.2), 52.0% ± 6.0% (Kv3.3), and 10.0% ± 1.6% (Kv3.4; for data see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and summary statistics).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

source: The percent contribution of each subunit gene to the cochlear nucleus Kv3 mRNA was 30.3% ± 9.1% (Kv3.1), 7.7% ± 2.8% (Kv3.2), 52.0% ± 6.0% (Kv3.3), and 10.0% ± 1.6% (Kv3.4; for data see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and summary statistics).
