source: These values are similar to those measured in the MNTB (Choudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: Both spiral ganglion neurons and cochlear nucleus have broad neuronal staining for Kv3.1 and Kv3.3.
source: Additionally, immunohistochemistry confirmed that both spiral ganglion neurons and cochlear nucleus have broad neuronal staining for Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 and as validated using tissue from knockout mice (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Low concentrations of extracellular TEA (1 mM) give a relatively selective block of Kv3 potassium channels.
source: Low concentrations of extracellular TEA (1 mM) give a relatively selective block of Kv3 potassium channels (Johnston et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnston et al., 2010 and represents established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: 1 mM TEA blocked 28.7% of the total outward current at a command voltage of +10 mV in WT calyces.
source: Whole terminal voltage-clamp recordings of the calyx terminal revealed an outward current, as shown in the current-voltage relations in Figure 1A, with 1 mM TEA blocking 28.7% of the total outward current at a command voltage of +10 mV (current amplitude in WT = 9.37 ± 2.6 nA, n=7 calyces; WT+TEA = 6.68±0.9 nA, n=6; unpaired t-test, p=0.037; mean ± SD).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mean AP half-width in WT calyces increased from 0.28±0.02ms (control) to 0.51±0.1ms in the presence of 1 mM TEA.
source: In tissue from WT mice the mean AP half-width increased from 0.28±0.02ms (control; n=9) to 0.51±0.1ms (n=7) in the presence of 1 mM TEA (Figure 1E), supporting the hypothesis that presynaptic Kv3 channels are present and contribute to AP repolarisation at the calyx of Held.
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Presynaptic Kv3 channels are present and contribute to AP repolarisation at the calyx of Held.
source: In tissue from WT mice the mean AP half-width increased from 0.28±0.02ms (control; n=9) to 0.51±0.1ms (n=7) in the presence of 1 mM TEA (Figure 1E), supporting the hypothesis that presynaptic Kv3 channels are present and contribute to AP repolarisation at the calyx of Held.
evidence: This is supported by the TEA effect on AP duration shown in Figure 1E and represents an inference from the data.

claim: AP half-widths increased from 0.28±0.02ms in WT to 0.43±0.03ms in Kv3.3KO mice.
source: AP half-widths increased from 0.28±0.02ms in WT (n=9) and 0.32±0.02ms Kv3.1KOs (n=5) to 0.43±0.03ms in Kv3.3KO mice (n=6) and 0.51±0.1ms in WT+TEA (n=7).
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AP half-width in Kv3.1KOs was 0.32±0.02ms.
source: AP half-widths increased from 0.28±0.02ms in WT (n=9) and 0.32±0.02ms Kv3.1KOs (n=5) to 0.43±0.03ms in Kv3.3KO mice (n=6) and 0.51±0.1ms in WT+TEA (n=7).
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The increase in AP duration at 50% amplitude was accompanied by a slowed rate of AP decay in both Kv3.3KO terminals and WT terminals upon perfusion of TEA.
source: This increase in duration at 50% amplitude was accompanied by a slowed rate of AP decay in both Kv3.3KO terminals and WT terminals upon perfusion of TEA (Figure 1G, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0042; TEA vs WT p=0.0016) with no changes in the rising phase of the AP (one-way ANOVA, p=0.50; Figure 1H), nor in the resting (input) membrane conductance (one-way ANOVA, p=0.56; Figure 1I) or AP threshold (one-way ANOVA, p=0.96; see statistics table).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There were no changes in the rising phase of the AP in Kv3.3KO or with TEA treatment.
source: This increase in duration at 50% amplitude was accompanied by a slowed rate of AP decay in both Kv3.3KO terminals and WT terminals upon perfusion of TEA (Figure 1G, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0042; TEA vs WT p=0.0016) with no changes in the rising phase of the AP (one-way ANOVA, p=0.50; Figure 1H), nor in the resting (input) membrane conductance (one-way ANOVA, p=0.56; Figure 1I) or AP threshold (one-way ANOVA, p=0.96; see statistics table).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There were no changes in the resting (input) membrane conductance in Kv3.3KO or with TEA treatment.
source: This increase in duration at 50% amplitude was accompanied by a slowed rate of AP decay in both Kv3.3KO terminals and WT terminals upon perfusion of TEA (Figure 1G, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0042; TEA vs WT p=0.0016) with no changes in the rising phase of the AP (one-way ANOVA, p=0.50; Figure 1H), nor in the resting (input) membrane conductance (one-way ANOVA, p=0.56; Figure 1I) or AP threshold (one-way ANOVA, p=0.96; see statistics table).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There were no changes in AP threshold in Kv3.3KO or with TEA treatment.
source: This increase in duration at 50% amplitude was accompanied by a slowed rate of AP decay in both Kv3.3KO terminals and WT terminals upon perfusion of TEA (Figure 1G, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0042; TEA vs WT p=0.0016) with no changes in the rising phase of the AP (one-way ANOVA, p=0.50; Figure 1H), nor in the resting (input) membrane conductance (one-way ANOVA, p=0.56; Figure 1I) or AP threshold (one-way ANOVA, p=0.96; see statistics table).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.1 did not significantly change AP duration at 25%, 50%, or 75% amplitude.
source: Similar significant changes in AP duration were observed at 25% and 75% amplitudes for deletion of Kv3.3, but deletion of Kv3.1 did not significantly change AP duration at 25%, 50%, or 75% amplitude (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Kv3.3 subunits are of most importance for presynaptic Kv3 channels and fast AP repolarisation.
source: This suggests that Kv3.3 subunits are of most importance for presynaptic Kv3 channels and fast AP repolarisation .
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Kv3.3 vs Kv3.1 deletion on AP duration.

claim: The rate of AP decay was significantly slowed in Kv3.1KOs from 99±20 mV/ms to 66±16 mV/ms.
source: Despite the lack of a significant increase in action potential duration measured in Kv3.1KOs, the rate of decay was significantly slowed from 99±20 mV/ms (n=10) to 66±16 mV/ms (n=5; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, p=0.02), consistent with Kv3.1 having a secondary role in presynaptic AP repolarisation, as might be expected from their localisation at axonal nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and potential to form heteromers with Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Kv3.1 has a secondary role in presynaptic AP repolarisation.
source: Despite the lack of a significant increase in action potential duration measured in Kv3.1KOs, the rate of decay was significantly slowed from 99±20 mV/ms (n=10) to 66±16 mV/ms (n=5; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, p=0.02), consistent with Kv3.1 having a secondary role in presynaptic AP repolarisation, as might be expected from their localisation at axonal nodes of Ranvier (Devaux et al., 2003) and potential to form heteromers with Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citation to Devaux et al., 2003.

claim: Electron microscopic studies demonstrated that Kv3.1b is present in the membrane of the non-release face of the calyx of Held.
source: Electron microscopic studies demonstrated that Kv3.1b is present in the membrane of the non-release face of the calyx of Held (Elezgarai et al., 2003), while Wu et al., 2021 show that Kv3.3 is present at the release face of the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elezgarai et al., 2003.

claim: Kv3.3 is present at the release face of the calyx.
source: Electron microscopic studies demonstrated that Kv3.1b is present in the membrane of the non-release face of the calyx of Held (Elezgarai et al., 2003), while Wu et al., 2021 show that Kv3.3 is present at the release face of the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2021.

claim: Kv3.3 has been demonstrated at terminals in the medial vestibular nucleus.
source: Kv3.3 has also been demonstrated at terminals in the medial vestibular nucleus (Brooke et al., 2010) at the neuromuscular junction (Brooke et al., 2004) and in hippocampal mossy fibers (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brooke et al., 2010.

claim: Kv3.3 has been demonstrated at the neuromuscular junction.
source: Kv3.3 has also been demonstrated at terminals in the medial vestibular nucleus (Brooke et al., 2010) at the neuromuscular junction (Brooke et al., 2004) and in hippocampal mossy fibers (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brooke et al., 2004.

claim: Kv3.3 has been demonstrated in hippocampal mossy fibers.
source: Kv3.3 has also been demonstrated at terminals in the medial vestibular nucleus (Brooke et al., 2010) at the neuromuscular junction (Brooke et al., 2004) and in hippocampal mossy fibers (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: Kv3.3 staining was clearly present in the presynaptic terminal profiles surrounding MNTB neurons which lacked Kv3.1.
source: Kv3.3 staining was clearly present in the presynaptic terminal profiles surrounding each of the 3 MNTB neurons which lacked Kv3.1 (Figure 2A1–C1).
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2A1–C1.

claim: Kv3.1 labelling showed little evidence of presynaptic labelling in Kv3.3KO tissue.
source: In contrast, Kv3.1 labelling (from the Kv3.3KO tissue) showed little evidence of presynaptic labelling (Figure 2D1–F1).
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2D1–F1.

claim: Kv3.1 labelling was robust in the postsynaptic membrane.
source: As a positive control, Kv3.1 labelling was robust in the postsynaptic membrane; and indeed Kv3.3 is also clearly present in the postsynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kv3.3 is clearly present in the postsynaptic membrane.
source: As a positive control, Kv3.1 labelling was robust in the postsynaptic membrane; and indeed Kv3.3 is also clearly present in the postsynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kv3.3 antibody staining was clearly observed in the presynaptic membrane on the non-release face of the WT synapse.
source: The Kv3.3 antibody staining was clearly observed in the presynaptic membrane on the non-release face of the WT synapse (for example see Figure 2B2 and C3, A6) and in some image sections the release face of the synapse, between bassoon labelling (see Figure 2C3, B5 and A6) was clear.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2B2, C3, and A6.

claim: Kv3.3 antibody staining was observed on the release face of the synapse, between bassoon labelling in some WT image sections.
source: The Kv3.3 antibody staining was clearly observed in the presynaptic membrane on the non-release face of the WT synapse (for example see Figure 2B2 and C3, A6) and in some image sections the release face of the synapse, between bassoon labelling (see Figure 2C3, B5 and A6) was clear.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2C3, B5, and A6.

claim: It was hard to visualise presynaptic membrane staining with the Kv3.1 antibody in the Kv3.3KO tissue.
source: It was hard to visualise presynaptic membrane staining with the Kv3.1 antibody in the Kv3.3KO tissue (Figure 2D2, E3 and F2); but some Kv3.1-stained membrane profiles were observed on the non-release face in the WT tissue (Figure 2E5, E6 and F6).
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2D2, E3, and F2.

claim: Some Kv3.1-stained membrane profiles were observed on the non-release face in the WT tissue.
source: It was hard to visualise presynaptic membrane staining with the Kv3.1 antibody in the Kv3.3KO tissue (Figure 2D2, E3 and F2); but some Kv3.1-stained membrane profiles were observed on the non-release face in the WT tissue (Figure 2E5, E6 and F6).
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2E5, E6, and F6.

claim: The levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher than in the Kv3.3KO.
source: While the calyceal Kv3.3 staining in the WT is similar to that in the Kv3.1KO, the levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher (than in the Kv3.3KO) consistent with the hypothesis that Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of immunostaining patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
source: While the calyceal Kv3.3 staining in the WT is similar to that in the Kv3.1KO, the levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher (than in the Kv3.3KO) consistent with the hypothesis that Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the immunostaining patterns and represents speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal.
source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential localization patterns observed in the knockout mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal.
source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kv3.1 staining is higher in WT than in Kv3.3KO presynaptic terminals.

claim: Both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2.

claim: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs.
source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs.
source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay tau data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Larger and longer lasting EPSCs in Kv3.3KO are consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held.
source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSC characteristics shown in Figure 3.

claim: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT (–13±2 nA) and Kv3.1KO (–14±2 nA).
source: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT and Kv3.1KO, –13±2 nA (n=21) and –14±2 nA (n=17), respectively; but increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EPSC amplitude increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA.
source: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT and Kv3.1KO, –13±2 nA (n=21) and –14±2 nA (n=17), respectively; but increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The decay tau for the EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO slowed to 0.23±0.06ms compared to 0.17±0.04ms in WT.
source: The decay tau for the EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO slowed to 0.23±0.06ms (n=21) compared to 0.17±0.04ms in WT (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, p=0.0012).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay tau data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The total charge of EPSCs in Kv3.3KOs increased to –10±4 nC compared to –6±1 nC in WT.
source: The total charge of EPSCs in Kv3.3KOs increased to –10±4 nC (n=21) compared to –6±1 nC and –7±2 nC in WT (n=21) and Kv3.1KOs (n=17), respectively (one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc; Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0007).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC charge data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No change of EPSC rise time was observed in either KO.
source: No change of EPSC rise time was observed in either KO (one-way ANOVA, p=0.1918).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC rise time data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a small significant decrease in mEPSC quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT.
source: Examination of miniature EPSCs in postsynaptic MNTB neurons from each genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed no difference in the mEPSC frequency, rise-time or decay tau. There was a small significant decrease in quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT, but no change in the Kv3.1KO.
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no change in mEPSC quantal amplitude in the Kv3.1KO.
source: Examination of miniature EPSCs in postsynaptic MNTB neurons from each genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed no difference in the mEPSC frequency, rise-time or decay tau. There was a small significant decrease in quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT, but no change in the Kv3.1KO.
evidence: This is supported by mEPSC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decreased mEPSC amplitude in Kv3.3KO perhaps reflects an opposing change in synaptic scaling due to the larger transmitter release.
source: This contrasts with the increased amplitude of the evoked EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO measured here, and perhaps reflects an opposing change in synaptic scaling due to the larger transmitter release induced in the Kv3.3KO (Tatavarty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to Tatavarty et al., 2013.

claim: Blocking presynaptic Kv3 channels with TEA had a much smaller effect on EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.3 KO compared to WT and Kv3.1 KO.
source: Indeed, blocking Kv3 channels with TEA had a much smaller effect on EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.3 KO compared to WT and Kv3.1 KO.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: TEA increased EPSC amplitude to 160% ± 33% in WT, compared to 114% ± 6% in Kv3.3KO.
source: TEA increased EPSC amplitude to 160% ± 33% (n=8) in WT, compared to 114% ± 6% (n=6) in Kv3.3KO (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's multiple comparison, p=0.0031).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.1KO (136% ± 11%) was not significantly different from WT in response to TEA.
source: The EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.1KO (136% ± 11%, n=4) was not significantly different from WT (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's multiple comparison p=0.99).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The reduced TEA effect in Kv3.3KO is consistent with dominance of presynaptic repolarisation by channels containing Kv3.3.
source: This result is consistent with dominance of presynaptic repolarisation by channels containing Kv3.3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TEA data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: The calyx of Held/MNTB synapse is capable of sustained transmission at firing frequencies of around 300 Hz in vivo.
source: The calyx of Held/MNTB synapse is capable of sustained transmission at firing frequencies of around 300 Hz in vivo (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2008) (also see Figure 8), encoding information about sound stimuli for binaural integration with high temporal precision.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2008 and by in vivo data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The calyx of Held giant synapse can sustain short AP bursts with peak firing rates of up to 1000 Hz in vitro for a few milliseconds.
source: Indeed, the calyx of Held giant synapse can sustain short AP bursts with peak firing rates of up to 1000 Hz, in vitro (Kim et al., 2013) for a few milliseconds.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claim: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO.
source: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO and subsequent EPSCs showed a larger short-term depression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Subsequent EPSCs in Kv3.3KO showed a larger short-term depression than WT or Kv3.1KO.
source: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO and subsequent EPSCs showed a larger short-term depression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C and quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: Paired pulse ratio (PPR) was significantly decreased in the Kv3.3KO compared to both WT and Kv3.1KO at 100 Hz, 200 Hz, and 600 Hz.
source: Paired pulse ratio (PPR) was significantly decreased in the Kv3.3KO compared to both WT and Kv3.1KO at 100 Hz, 200 Hz, and 600 Hz, with mean PPR (EPSC2/EPSC1) plotted in Figure 4D (left column).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: Enhanced depression of EPSC amplitude was maintained for the duration of the train in Kv3.3KO.
source: This enhanced depression of EPSC amplitude was maintained for the duration of the train shown in comparison with the 80th EPSC in the train (EPSC80/EPSC1; Figure 4D, right column; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: The Kv3.3KO consistently showed the fastest rate of short-term depression, compared to WT and Kv3.1KOs.
source: The Kv3.3KO consistently showed the fastest rate of short-term depression, compared to WT and Kv3.1KOs; this was highly significant at 100 Hz and 200 Hz (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–G and Table 1.

claim: The decay time-constant for short-term depression at 600 Hz was 6±1ms for Kv3.3KOs, 11±2ms for WT and 20±13ms for Kv3.1KOs.
source: The decay time-constant for short-term depression was 6±1ms for Kv3.3KOs (n=8), 11±2ms for WT (n=10) and 20±13ms for Kv3.1KOs (n=5; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Table 1.

claim: At all frequencies, EPSCs from the Kv3.3KO mice showed lower amplitude steady-state values in comparison to WT.
source: At all frequencies, EPSCs from the Kv3.3KO mice showed lower amplitude steady-state values in comparison to WT; while the Kv3.1KO data was either the same or greater than WT (Figure 4E, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–G and Table 1.

claim: Presynaptic spike broadening has been shown to enhance vesicle recycling during repetitive stimulation trains due to enhanced calcium-dependent recovery.
source: Presynaptic spike broadening has previously been shown to enhance vesicle recycling during repetitive stimulation trains (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) due to enhanced calcium-dependent recovery.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998.

claim: The fast time-constant of recovery was significantly accelerated in the Kv3.3KO (0.2±0.2 s) compared to WT (0.45±0.2 s) and Kv3.1KO (0.4±0.2 s).
source: The fast time-constant was significantly accelerated in the Kv3.3KO compared to WT and Kv3.1KO (0.2±0.2 s in Kv3.3KO; 0.45±0.2 s in WT and 0.4±0.2 s in the Kv3.1KO; Figure 5F, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The slow time-constant of recovery was 5±3 s in WT, and was similar to both Kv3.1KO and Kv3.3KO.
source: The slow time-constant was 5±3 s in WT, and was similar to both Kv3.1KO and Kv3.3KO (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The enhanced fast recovery rate is consistent with an activity-dependent component of vesicle recycling.
source: The enhanced fast recovery rate is consistent with an activity-dependent component of vesicle recycling as observed previously on blocking presynaptic Kv3 channels at the calyx of Held (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) and as recently attributed to Ca2+-phospholipid-dependent vesicle priming (Lipstein et al., 2021) via Munc13-1.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998 and Lipstein et al., 2021.

claim: The dominant change in the model parameters between WT and Kv3.3KO was an increase in the probability of vesicular release (Pv) from 0.13 in WT to 0.266 in the Kv3.3KO.
source: The table in Figure 6B shows that the dominant change in the model parameters between WT and Kv3.3KO, was an increase in the probability of vesicular release (Pv) from 0.13 in WT to 0.266 in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a 20% acceleration of the replenishment rate (smaller τh) in Kv3.3KO.
source: There was also evidence for an increase in activity-dependent recycling, with a 20% acceleration of the replenishment rate (smaller τh in Kv3.3KO).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh.
source: This model showed that the physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh (higher recycling rate), both of which are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP (see Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6 and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Both increased Pv and decreased τh are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP.
source: This model showed that the physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh (higher recycling rate), both of which are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP (see Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021.

claim: MNTB AP output in response to high frequency calyceal EPSC input declines with both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 deletion.
source: The initial observation was that MNTB AP output in response to high frequency calyceal EPSC input, declines with both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 deletion (Figure 7A) when measured over the whole train (WT: 52.49% ± 8.15%, n=5; Kv3.3KO: 29.8% ± 10.43%, n=7; Kv3.1KO: 36.29% ± 11.12%, n=6; Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0044, Kv3.1KO vs WT p=0.046, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There are three phases of AP firing to evoked trains of calyceal synaptic responses.
source: But closer inspection reveals three phases of AP firing to evoked trains of calyceal synaptic responses as illustrated in Figure 7B.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Phase I, every evoked EPSP triggered one MNTB AP.
source: In Phase I (green trace, Figure 7B) which predominates at the start of each train, every evoked EPSP triggered one MNTB AP: so the MNTB output matched the calyx input.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Phase II, EPSPs often failed to evoke an AP, and the MNTB AP firing becomes chaotic and unpredictable.
source: Firing then transitioned to Phase II (blue trace, Figure 7B) after around 6–9 stimuli, where EPSPs often failed to evoke an AP, and the MNTB AP firing becomes chaotic, unpredictable and poorly transmits the timing information contained within the presynaptic AP train.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In Phase III, the MNTB neuron fired APs to alternate EPSPs.
source: In Phase III (black trace, Figure 7B): the EPSP had undergone short-term depression and approached a 'steady-state' amplitude; now the MNTB neuron fired APs to alternate EPSPs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: At frequencies up to 200 Hz the duration of Phase I was essentially identical across the three genotypes.
source: At frequencies up to 200 Hz the duration of Phase I was essentially identical across the three genotypes (Figure 7C), all showed 100% firing throughout the train; then from 300 Hz and above, the Phase I duration declined dramatically for all genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At 600 Hz stimulation frequency, only 1 out of 6 calyx/MNTB pairs in Kv3.3KO briefly entered Phase III firing.
source: The latency for Phase III was similar in WT and Kv3.1KO (510±224ms and 597±251ms, respectively) but in the Kv3.3KO only 1 out of 6 calyx/MNTB pairs briefly entered Phase III firing (Kv3.3KO vs WT Phase II p=0.0135, Phase III p=0.02, two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Presynaptic Kv3.3 and fast presynaptic APs serve a role in maintaining information transmission across the synapse during high frequency firing.
source: This is consistent with the idea that presynaptic Kv3.3 and hence fast presynaptic APs, serve a role in maintaining information transmission across the synapse during high frequency firing, when short APs conserve resources, and slow the rate of short-term depression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Phase III firing data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the Kv3.1KO, calyceal stimulation evoked a sustained depolarisation at frequencies above 100 Hz.
source: However, in the Kv3.1KO, calyceal stimulation evoked a sustained depolarisation (in addition to EPSPs) at frequencies above 100 Hz (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The plateau depolarisation was significantly larger for the Kv3.1KO at frequencies above 100 Hz.
source: Although all genotypes exhibited this plateau depolarisation at 600 Hz, it was significantly larger for the Kv3.1KO at frequencies above 100 Hz (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Kv3.3KOs showed a reduced plateau potential at frequencies above 300 Hz, reaching significance only at 600 Hz.
source: In contrast, Kv3.3KOs showed a reduced plateau potential at frequencies above 300 Hz, reaching significance only at 600 Hz (Figure 7F; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The time to half-decay of the depolarisation following the end of the train was significantly longer in the Kv3.1KO (15.96±8.59ms) compared to WT (2.79±1.73ms).
source: This was also observed as a decaying depolarisation at the end of the train (Figure 7G), with the time to half-decay plotted in Figure 7H (WT: 2.79±1.73ms, n=7: Kv3.3KO: 1.89±0.92ms, n=6: Kv3.1KO: 15.96±8.59ms, n=8: Kv3.1KO vs WT p=0. 000553, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, the decay of depolarisation was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant.
source: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, this decay was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant, but in the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of decay kinetics with membrane time constants.

claim: In the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
source: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, this decay was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant, but in the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
evidence: This is supported by observation of the data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The EPSC decay time constants for all genotypes were essentially identical.
source: The EPSC decay time constants for all genotypes were essentially identical, consistent with no change in glutamate receptor expression (WT: 2.74±1.26ms, n=8; Kv3.3KO: 3.1±0.87ms, n=8; Kv3.1KO: 3.54±0.9ms, n=6).
evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay time constant measurements.

claim: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) thresholds were similar in 6-month-old WT and Kv3.3KO mice.
source: Behaviourally, the Kv3.3KO mouse is as sensitive to sound as the WT in that Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) thresholds were similar in 6-month-old WT and Kv3.3KO mice, with no statistical difference across a wide frequency range (see summary statistics, unpaired t-test with Holm-Šídák's test for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by ABR threshold measurements.

claim: ABR waveform analysis showed significant deficits in Wave IV at 6 months in Kv3.3KO which were not apparent at 1 month of age.
source: However, further analysis of the ABR waveform showed significant deficits in Wave IV at 6 months which were not apparent in recordings taken at 1 month of age.
evidence: This is supported by ABR waveform analysis.

claim: A developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III.
source: We have previously demonstrated that a developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III (Jalabi et al., 2013), so the decrease in Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem and is being characterized as part of another study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jalabi et al., 2013.

claim: The decrease in ABR Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem.
source: We have previously demonstrated that a developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III (Jalabi et al., 2013), so the decrease in Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem and is being characterized as part of another study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and the ABR data.

claim: AP halfwidth of the presynaptic AP was significantly longer in Kv3.3KOs (0.25ms) compared to WT recordings (0.17ms).
source: AP halfwidth of the presynaptic AP (preAP) was significantly longer in Kv3.3KOs (0.25ms [0.16; 0.31]; n=13) compared to WT recordings (0.17ms [0.16; 0.19]; n=20; Figure 8B; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.036).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Synaptic delays were significantly prolonged in Kv3.3KOs (0.56ms) compared to WT controls (0.44ms).
source: Synaptic delays as measured by peak-to-peak times in the complex waveform were also significantly prolonged in Kv3.3KOs (0.56ms [0.45; 0.70]; n=13) compared to WT controls (0.44ms [0.41; 0.49]; n=20; Figure 8C; n=13; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.013).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Postsynaptic AP duration was prolonged in the Kv3.3KOs (0.64ms) compared to WT (0.36ms).
source: While changes in presynaptic AP duration and synaptic delay may predominantly affect temporal processing, the prolonged postsynaptic AP duration observed in the Kv3.3KOs (0.64ms [0.29; 0.46]; n=13; Figure 8D) might influence high-frequency firing abilities (WT: 0.36ms [0.48; 0.82]; n=20; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p≤0.001).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Kv3.3KO neurons were slower to respond to sound with first spike latencies of 4.06ms compared to 3.44ms in WT.
source: In contrast, Kv3.3KO neurons were slower to respond to sound with first spike latencies of 4.06ms [3.01; 4.21] (n=25; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.015; Figure 8I and J) and showed larger temporal variability (0.92ms [0.56; 1.50]; n=18; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.001; Figure 8I and K).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8I and J.

claim: Kv3.3KO neurons showed larger temporal variability (jitter of 0.92ms) compared to WT (0.18ms).
source: In contrast, Kv3.3KO neurons were slower to respond to sound with first spike latencies of 4.06ms [3.01; 4.21] (n=25; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.015; Figure 8I and J) and showed larger temporal variability (0.92ms [0.56; 1.50]; n=18; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.001; Figure 8I and K).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8I and K.

claim: The average inter-spike intervals shifted from 2.16ms in WT to 3.10ms in the Kv3.3KO.
source: The inability to fire high instantaneous rates at sound onset was accompanied by a shift in the average inter-spike intervals from 2.16ms [1.48; 3.57] (n=22) in the WT to 3.10ms [2.49; 4.19] (n=18) in the Kv3.3KO (Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p≤0.001; Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Peak firing rates during the first 10ms of the sound-evoked response were significantly lower in Kv3.3KOs (240 Hz) compared to WTs (350 Hz).
source: Indeed, comparing peak firing rates during the first 10ms of the sound-evoked response revealed significantly lower rates in Kv3.3KOs (240 Hz [180; 280]; n=18) compared to WTs (350 Hz [200; 425]; n=22; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.003; Figure 8H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: An increase in spontaneous firing was observed in the Kv3.3KOs (40 Hz) compared to WT controls (16.5 Hz).
source: In contrast to the reduced sound-evoked firing rates, an increase in spontaneous firing was observed in the Kv3.3KOs (Kv3.3KO: 40 Hz [19.3; 62.0]; n=19) compared to WT controls (16.5 Hz [4.5; 42.8]; n=24; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.044; Figure 8L).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8L.

claim: These combined changes caused a significant reduction in signal-to-noise ratio in the Kv3.3KO (2.77) compared to WT controls (9.70).
source: Together, these combined changes caused a significant reduction in signal-to-noise ratio in the Kv3.3KO (2.77 [2.04; 3.99]; n=14) compared to WT controls (9.70 [4.38; 40.95]; n=18; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.001; Figure 8M).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8M.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.3 subunits increased presynaptic AP duration and transmitter release, enhancing short-term depression on repetitive stimulation.
source: Deletion of Kv3.3 subunits increased presynaptic AP duration and transmitter release, enhancing short-term depression on repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the integration of multiple experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of Kv3.1 had little effect on the presynaptic AP or transmitter release.
source: In contrast, deletion of Kv3.1 had little effect on the presynaptic AP or transmitter release.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The enhanced short-term depression of synaptic responses increased latency jitter and reduced postsynaptic AP firing at high frequencies in the Kv3.3KO.
source: The enhanced short-term depression of synaptic responses increased latency jitter and reduced postsynaptic AP firing (output) at high frequencies in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In vivo, deletion of Kv3.3 manifests as reduced temporal fidelity and firing rates in the binaural auditory circuit in response to sound.
source: In vivo this manifests as reduced temporal fidelity and firing rates in the binaural auditory circuit in response to sound, whilst spontaneous AP firing increased in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the in vivo data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Spontaneous AP firing increased in the Kv3.3KO in vivo.
source: In vivo this manifests as reduced temporal fidelity and firing rates in the binaural auditory circuit in response to sound, whilst spontaneous AP firing increased in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data shown in Figure 8L.

claim: The magnitude and fast kinetics of Kv3 channels guarantee fast repolarisation and generate a fast afterhyperpolarisation.
source: The magnitude and fast kinetics of Kv3 channels guarantee fast repolarisation and generate a fast afterhyperpolarisation (Brew and Forsythe, 1995; Figure 1B, here) which in concert with a resurgent Na+ current (Kim et al., 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014) maximizes the availability of voltage-gated Na+ channels to maintain short APs during sustained firing, as also observed in vivo (Sierksma and Borst, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brew and Forsythe, 1995; Kim et al., 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014; Sierksma and Borst, 2017 and by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Kv3 channels in concert with a resurgent Na+ current maximize the availability of voltage-gated Na+ channels to maintain short APs during sustained firing.
source: The magnitude and fast kinetics of Kv3 channels guarantee fast repolarisation and generate a fast afterhyperpolarisation (Brew and Forsythe, 1995; Figure 1B, here) which in concert with a resurgent Na+ current (Kim et al., 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014) maximizes the availability of voltage-gated Na+ channels to maintain short APs during sustained firing, as also observed in vivo (Sierksma and Borst, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2010; Lewis and Raman, 2014; Sierksma and Borst, 2017.

claim: The increase in transmitter release in Kv3.3KO is primarily an increase in vesicle release probability.
source: Our modelling indicates that the increase in transmitter release is primarily an increase in vesicle release probability (and subsequent short-term depression) but an acceleration of vesicle recycling also contributes.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: An acceleration of vesicle recycling contributes to the increase in transmitter release in Kv3.3KO.
source: Our modelling indicates that the increase in transmitter release is primarily an increase in vesicle release probability (and subsequent short-term depression) but an acceleration of vesicle recycling also contributes.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The calyx of Held undergoes a range of developmental changes that foster temporally accurate transmission.
source: The calyx of Held undergoes a range of developmental changes that foster temporally accurate transmission (Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Presynaptic calcium channels shift from N to P/Q type during development.
source: Presynaptic calcium channels shift from N to P/Q type (Iwasaki et al., 2000), myelination induces developmental and activity-dependent changes (Kim et al., 2013; Sinclair et al., 2017) and similar adaptations favouring high-frequency firing are occurring in neonatal rat pups (Sierksma and Borst, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwasaki et al., 2000.

claim: Myelination induces developmental and activity-dependent changes at the calyx of Held.
source: Presynaptic calcium channels shift from N to P/Q type (Iwasaki et al., 2000), myelination induces developmental and activity-dependent changes (Kim et al., 2013; Sinclair et al., 2017) and similar adaptations favouring high-frequency firing are occurring in neonatal rat pups (Sierksma and Borst, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Sinclair et al., 2017.

claim: The AP time-course accelerates during development.
source: The AP time-course accelerates (Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000) with increased expression of Nav1.6 (Leão et al., 2005) which in turn influences activation of the voltage-gated calcium channels (Borst and Sakmann, 1998) and hence the efficacy of transmitter release (Yang and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000.

claim: Increased expression of Nav1.6 occurs during development.
source: The AP time-course accelerates (Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000) with increased expression of Nav1.6 (Leão et al., 2005) which in turn influences activation of the voltage-gated calcium channels (Borst and Sakmann, 1998) and hence the efficacy of transmitter release (Yang and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leão et al., 2005.

claim: Nav1.6 expression influences activation of the voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: The AP time-course accelerates (Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000) with increased expression of Nav1.6 (Leão et al., 2005) which in turn influences activation of the voltage-gated calcium channels (Borst and Sakmann, 1998) and hence the efficacy of transmitter release (Yang and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Borst and Sakmann, 1998.

claim: Nav1.6 expression influences the efficacy of transmitter release.
source: The AP time-course accelerates (Taschenberger and von Gersdorff, 2000) with increased expression of Nav1.6 (Leão et al., 2005) which in turn influences activation of the voltage-gated calcium channels (Borst and Sakmann, 1998) and hence the efficacy of transmitter release (Yang and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang and Wang, 2006.

claim: Presynaptic Kv currents increase during development with the major change being before hearing onset.
source: Presynaptic Kv currents also increase (Nakamura and Takahashi, 2007) with the major change being before hearing onset (and little change from P13 to P20).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakamura and Takahashi, 2007.

claim: A concurrent switch to fast time-course GluA4-flop dominated AMPAR-mediated EPSCs occurs at the postsynaptic membrane during development.
source: At the post-synaptic membrane, a concurrent switch to fast time-course GluA4-flop dominated AMPAR-mediated EPSCs (Barnes-Davies and Forsythe, 1995; Geiger et al., 1995; Yang et al., 2011) with developmental refinement in GluA2, reducing calcium permeability (Lujan et al., 2019) and a decrease in AMPAR desensitisation, further enhance transmission fidelity (Taschenberger et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barnes-Davies and Forsythe, 1995; Geiger et al., 1995; Yang et al., 2011.

claim: Developmental refinement in GluA2 reduces calcium permeability.
source: At the post-synaptic membrane, a concurrent switch to fast time-course GluA4-flop dominated AMPAR-mediated EPSCs (Barnes-Davies and Forsythe, 1995; Geiger et al., 1995; Yang et al., 2011) with developmental refinement in GluA2, reducing calcium permeability (Lujan et al., 2019) and a decrease in AMPAR desensitisation, further enhance transmission fidelity (Taschenberger et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lujan et al., 2019.

claim: A decrease in AMPAR desensitisation enhances transmission fidelity.
source: At the post-synaptic membrane, a concurrent switch to fast time-course GluA4-flop dominated AMPAR-mediated EPSCs (Barnes-Davies and Forsythe, 1995; Geiger et al., 1995; Yang et al., 2011) with developmental refinement in GluA2, reducing calcium permeability (Lujan et al., 2019) and a decrease in AMPAR desensitisation, further enhance transmission fidelity (Taschenberger et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taschenberger et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2003.

claim: Kv3.3 remains crucial in shaping the presynaptic AP waveform and neurotransmitter release at the calyx over a wide age range from P10-P12 to 6 months old.
source: The present study interrogates the role of Kv3 subunits over a wide age range, from a relatively immature calyx (P10-P12) to mature adult (6 months old) and despite the inevitable developmental changes during this period, Kv3.3 remains crucial in shaping the presynaptic AP waveform and neurotransmitter release at the calyx.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data collected across different developmental stages.

claim: An increase in Kv3 expression with age may amplify the deficits observed in Kv3.3KOs at later developmental stages.
source: An increase in Kv3 expression with age may actually amplify the deficits observed in Kv3.3KOs at later developmental stages however this study shows that even with a small deficiency in Kv3.3 expression in young Kv3.3KO animals, there are drastic consequences at the synapse.
evidence: This is speculation about the developmental trajectory.

claim: Even with a small deficiency in Kv3.3 expression in young Kv3.3KO animals, there are drastic consequences at the synapse.
source: An increase in Kv3 expression with age may actually amplify the deficits observed in Kv3.3KOs at later developmental stages however this study shows that even with a small deficiency in Kv3.3 expression in young Kv3.3KO animals, there are drastic consequences at the synapse.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data from young animals.

claim: Kv channel building is regulated by the N-terminal tetramerisation domain (T1).
source: Kv channel building is regulated by the N-terminal tetramerisation domain (T1) (Li et al., 1992) to favour assembly of 'dimers of dimers' (Tu and Deutsch, 1999) usually from subunits within the same Kv family.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 1992; Tu and Deutsch, 1999 and represents established knowledge about Kv channel assembly.

claim: Kv3 subunits do not co-assemble with the accessory subunit gene families (Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, and Kv9).
source: Although early studies suggested otherwise, Kv3 subunits do not co-assemble with the accessory subunit gene families (Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, and Kv9) (Bocksteins et al., 2014), so Kv3 channels are likely composed of four Kv3 alpha subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bocksteins et al., 2014.

claim: Kv3 channels are likely composed of four Kv3 alpha subunits.
source: Although early studies suggested otherwise, Kv3 subunits do not co-assemble with the accessory subunit gene families (Kv5, Kv6, Kv8, and Kv9) (Bocksteins et al., 2014), so Kv3 channels are likely composed of four Kv3 alpha subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the citation to Bocksteins et al., 2014.

claim: Coimmunoprecipitation has revealed interactions of Kv3.1b with Kv3.4a and Kv3.2 in globus pallidus neurons.
source: Frequent co-expression of Kv3 subunits in the same neurons suggest functional channels could exist as heteromers, indeed coimmunoprecipitation has revealed interactions of Kv3.1b with Kv3.4a and Kv3.2 in globus pallidus neurons (Baranauskas et al., 2003; Hernández-Pineda et al., 1999), and with Kv3.3 in the cerebellum (Chang et al., 2007) but homomeric assemblies of Kv3.3 subunits could also form presynaptic Kv3 channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baranauskas et al., 2003; Hernández-Pineda et al., 1999.

claim: Coimmunoprecipitation has revealed interactions of Kv3.1b with Kv3.3 in the cerebellum.
source: Frequent co-expression of Kv3 subunits in the same neurons suggest functional channels could exist as heteromers, indeed coimmunoprecipitation has revealed interactions of Kv3.1b with Kv3.4a and Kv3.2 in globus pallidus neurons (Baranauskas et al., 2003; Hernández-Pineda et al., 1999), and with Kv3.3 in the cerebellum (Chang et al., 2007) but homomeric assemblies of Kv3.3 subunits could also form presynaptic Kv3 channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2007.

claim: Homomeric assemblies of Kv3.3 subunits could form presynaptic Kv3 channels.
source: Frequent co-expression of Kv3 subunits in the same neurons suggest functional channels could exist as heteromers, indeed coimmunoprecipitation has revealed interactions of Kv3.1b with Kv3.4a and Kv3.2 in globus pallidus neurons (Baranauskas et al., 2003; Hernández-Pineda et al., 1999), and with Kv3.3 in the cerebellum (Chang et al., 2007) but homomeric assemblies of Kv3.3 subunits could also form presynaptic Kv3 channels.
evidence: This is speculation about possible channel composition.

claim: Presynaptic Kv3 channels at the calyx of Held require an obligatory Kv3.3 subunit.
source: The data reported here suggests that presynaptic Kv3 channels at the calyx of Held require an obligatory Kv3.3 subunit, since TEA (which will block all Kv3 heteromers) showed little effect on transmission in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TEA data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Kv3.1 does not have a directive or independent role in the terminal.
source: This result also implies that Kv3.1 does not have a directive or independent role in the terminal and while heteromers with Kv3.3 may occur, Kv3.1 is certainly not required for Kv3.3 localisation to the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining and functional data.

claim: Kv3.1 is not required for Kv3.3 localisation to the presynaptic membrane.
source: This result also implies that Kv3.1 does not have a directive or independent role in the terminal and while heteromers with Kv3.3 may occur, Kv3.1 is certainly not required for Kv3.3 localisation to the presynaptic membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kv3.3 is present at presynaptic terminals in Kv3.1KO mice (Figure 2).

claim: Excitatory synaptic boutons show pharmacological evidence for presynaptic Kv3.
source: Excitatory synaptic boutons, including hippocampal mossy fiber terminals (Alle et al., 2011), cerebellar mossy fiber terminals (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014) and small neocortical boutons (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2021) show pharmacological evidence for presynaptic Kv3.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alle et al., 2011; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014; Ritzau-Jost et al., 2021.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons possess presynaptic Kv3 channels.
source: Inhibitory interneurons also possess presynaptic Kv3 channels, including cerebellar basket cell terminals (Southan and Robertson, 2000) and stellate cell axons (Rowan et al., 2016), with the latter being identified as Kv3.4.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Southan and Robertson, 2000; Rowan et al., 2016.

claim: It is unlikely that Kv3.4 (or Kv3.2) subunits have a directive (or independent) role in trafficking Kv3 channels to the calyx terminal.
source: It seems unlikely that Kv3.4 (or Kv3.2) subunits have a directive (or independent) role in trafficking Kv3 channels to the calyx terminal, since the mRNA levels for these subunits was very low in the MNTB and VCN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mRNA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: If Kv3.4 (or Kv3.2) were assembled into calyx Kv3 channels, then TEA should have enhanced transmitter release in the Kv3.3KO, but TEA potentiation of transmission was occluded in the Kv3.3KO.
source: However, if there were effective translation and assembly of Kv3.4 (or Kv3.2) into calyx Kv3 channels, then TEA should have enhanced transmitter release in the Kv3.3KO, but TEA potentiation of transmission was occluded in the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TEA data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Early studies of recombinant Kv3.3 showed N-type (ball-peptide) inactivation.
source: In contrast to Kv3.1 and Kv3.2, early studies of recombinant Kv3.3 showed N-type (ball-peptide) inactivation, as originally described for Kv1 potassium channels (Hoshi et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoshi et al., 1990 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Little or no inactivation of the presynaptic Kv3 current was observed at the calyx.
source: We conclude here that Kv3.3 is a principal component of presynaptic Kv3 channels but we observe little or no inactivation of the presynaptic Kv3 current.
evidence: This is based on the voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The degree of Kv3 inactivation varies between different expression systems.
source: There are multiple explanations for this lack of inactivation. The degree of Kv3 inactivation varies between different expression systems (Rudy et al., 1999), perhaps due to there being two methionine start codons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rudy et al., 1999.

claim: Mammals lack a well-defined Kozak consensus sequence for the first methionine in Kv3.3, favouring initiation at the second methionine, thereby excluding the N-terminal peptide.
source: Mammals lack a well-defined Kozak consensus sequence for the first, favouring initiation at the second methionine, thereby excluding the N-terminal peptide (Fernandez et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fernandez et al., 2003.

claim: Endogenous PKC phosphorylation of N-terminal Kv3.3 could occlude the N-type inactivation.
source: Alternatively, endogenous PKC phosphorylation of N-terminal Kv3.3 could occlude the N-type inactivation (Desai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Desai et al., 2008.

claim: Little or no inactivation was observed in the postsynaptic Kv3.3 channel.
source: Also, little or no inactivation was observed in the postsynaptic Kv3.3 channel (Choudhury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: It is unlikely that Kv3.4 subunits are present in the calyx terminal given the lack of inactivating current.
source: Given this lack of inactivating current observed at the calyx, it is unlikely that Kv3.4 subunits are present in this terminal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of inactivation in the recorded currents.

claim: In recombinant co-expression studies, Kv3.3 and Kv3.4 did not readily form heteromers.
source: Further to this, in recombinant co-expression studies, Kv3.3 and Kv3.4 did not readily form heteromers, but instead formed distinct currents with differing kinetics in the same cells (Richardson, Forsythe and Pilati, unpublished observations) suggesting that heteromeric channels composed of these subunits are unlikely.
evidence: This is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: Heteromeric channels composed of Kv3.3 and Kv3.4 subunits are unlikely.
source: Further to this, in recombinant co-expression studies, Kv3.3 and Kv3.4 did not readily form heteromers, but instead formed distinct currents with differing kinetics in the same cells (Richardson, Forsythe and Pilati, unpublished observations) suggesting that heteromeric channels composed of these subunits are unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on unpublished data.

claim: In terminals that exhibit inactivation of presynaptic potassium currents, this has important physiological implications for transmitter release, especially during sustained high-frequency AP firing.
source: In terminals that exhibit inactivation of presynaptic potassium currents, this has important physiological implications for transmitter release, especially during sustained high-frequency AP firing.
evidence: This represents general knowledge about the physiological consequences of channel inactivation.

claim: Repetitive activation during AP trains would cause cumulative Kv3 inactivation and progressively slows AP repolarisation.
source: Repetitive activation during AP trains would cause cumulative Kv3 inactivation and progressively slows AP repolarisation.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of inactivation.

claim: Cumulative Kv3 inactivation can generate a form of activity-dependent short-term potentiation where increasing AP duration potentiates transmitter release, as occurs at mossy fiber terminals.
source: This can generate a form of activity-dependent short-term potentiation where increasing AP duration potentiates transmitter release, as occurs at mossy fiber terminals (Geiger and Jonas, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geiger and Jonas, 2000.

claim: During sustained high-frequency AP firing at the calyx, a longer AP duration induced by an inactivating Kv3 would risk earlier transmission failure.
source: During sustained high-frequency AP firing at the calyx, the longer AP duration induced by an inactivating Kv3 would risk earlier transmission failure, with faster depletion of vesicles and inactivation of the presynaptic sodium channels.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of inactivation at this synapse.

claim: The physiological end-point for an inactivating Kv3 would be similar to that measured for the Kv3.3KO.
source: The physiological end-point for an inactivating Kv3 would be similar to that measured for the Kv3.3KO.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the Kv3.3KO phenotype with expected effects of inactivation.

claim: The minimal inactivation of the presynaptic Kv3 current at the calyx of Held enables transmission to be sustained for longer, at higher firing rates and greater accuracy.
source: Hence, the minimal inactivation of the presynaptic Kv3 current at the calyx of Held enables transmission to be sustained for longer, at higher firing rates and greater accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and the lack of inactivation.

claim: Proximity of K+ channels have powerful influences on the local voltage and therefore in control of other voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Proximity of K+ channels have powerful influences on the local voltage and therefore in control of other voltage-gated ion channels.
evidence: This represents general knowledge about ion channel function.

claim: The permutations and complexity of channel subunit assembly optimize function through subunit-specific localisation.
source: The permutations and complexity of channel subunit assembly optimize function through subunit-specific localisation (Trimmer, 2015) involving trafficking, insertion, phosphorylation, and stabilisation of channel complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Trimmer, 2015 and represents established knowledge.

claim: There is a well-established role for ankyrin-G in axonal targeting of Kv3.1b.
source: There is a well-established role for ankyrin-G in axonal targeting of Kv3.1b (Xu et al., 2007) and for clustering of sodium and potassium channels at the initial segment (Pan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2006.

claim: Ankyrin-R binds and stabilizes Kv3.1b in fast spiking interneuron somatic membranes and nodes of Ranvier.
source: Ankyrin-R binds and stabilizes Kv3.1b in fast spiking interneuron somatic membranes and nodes of Ranvier; and crosslinks Kv3.3 via spectrin to the cytoskeleton in Purkinje neurons, which aids their survival (Stevens et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2022.

claim: Ankyrin-R crosslinks Kv3.3 via spectrin to the cytoskeleton in Purkinje neurons, which aids their survival.
source: Ankyrin-R binds and stabilizes Kv3.1b in fast spiking interneuron somatic membranes and nodes of Ranvier; and crosslinks Kv3.3 via spectrin to the cytoskeleton in Purkinje neurons, which aids their survival (Stevens et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2022.

claim: The interaction of both Kv3.1b and Kv3.3 with ankyrin-R would explain the inability of the MNTB neuron soma to differentiate or partition channels composed of these subunits.
source: This interaction of both subunits with ankyrin-R would explain the inability of the MNTB neuron soma to differentiate or partition channels composed of Kv3.1b or Kv3.3 subunits (Choudhury et al., 2020) so that each subunit type could largely compensate for the absence of the other within the soma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known interactions and the functional data from Choudhury et al., 2020.

claim: Presynaptic stabilisation of Kv3.3 is unlikely to be through ankyrin-R alone, as this mechanism would not discriminate between the subunits.
source: Presynaptic stabilisation of Kv3.3 however, is unlikely to be through ankyrin-R alone, as this mechanism would not discriminate between the subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential presynaptic localization observed.

claim: Kv3.3 inactivation may be suppressed by the C-terminus associating with Hax1 to bind the Kv3.3 N-Terminal ball peptide and modulate the actin network.

evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Blosa et al., 2015.

claim: The presynaptic K+ currents from a Kv3.3KO calyx were similar magnitude to WT in Zhang et al., 2016.
source: However, as in the WT, the calyceal outward currents reported in Zhang et al., 2016 were an order of magnitude smaller than observed here or elsewhere. Additionally, the presynaptic K+ currents from a Kv3.3KO calyx were similar magnitude to WT (Figure S4: Zhang et al., 2016).

evidence: This is a comparison with the Wu et al., 2021 study and represents an inference about the differences.

claim: At the highest frequencies only the first few presynaptic APs generate postsynaptic APs with 1:1 fidelity before entering a chaotic phase with many failures.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Tollin, 2003; Joris and Trussell, 2018 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The synaptic delay measured in this study was favourably comparable to other studies using different anesthetics.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting Kv3.3 localization.

claim: Presynaptic Kv3.3 would enhance resource and energy conservation during high frequency firing.
source: It is interesting to consider why Kv3.3 is present at some synaptic terminals, but not all. One hypothesis is that presynaptic Kv3.3 would enhance resource and energy conservation during high frequency firing, but more importantly it will support the physiological mechanisms as a synapse evolves from a microdomain to a nanodomain architecture for exocytosis (Meinrenken et al., 2003; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021) by constraining presynaptic calcium influx.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of Kv3.3.
